trait_value_raw: An entirely tropical family with worldwide distribution with 20 genera and c. 500 species
In Peninsular Malaysia, the family is represented by 5 genera with 66 species of which several are local endemics
The largest genera are Horsfieldia with 22 species and Knema with 27 species.
The Myristicaceae is a family of low or medium-sized, rarely canopy, trees in various types of primary lowland rain forest, including fresh water and peat swamp forest (elsewhere in kerangas)
Few species are montane, and few are found in secondary forest
Sometimes Myristicaceae constitute a considerable component of the forest, especially of the middle storey of lowland mixed dipterocarp forest, but they are not gregarious
Flowering and fruiting is generally throughout the year
The usually more-or-less fleshy, yellow or brown, inside creamy, pink, or red flowers of several genera have repeatedly been reported as being fragrant, e.g. Horsfieldia irya
Corner (1988) comments on its citron scent
Anthesis is presumably mainly nocturnal, and in some species small beetles effect pollination (Corlette, Biol
No nectar is reported for any species

Besides the coloured inside of the perianth, in Knema the staminal disc may also be brightly (purple-red) coloured, the contrast with the creamy-white pollen may possibly be connected with attraction of pollinators

The blackish seed contrasting with the red aril and the red, pink, or white inner surface of the opened pericarp attracts birds like fruit pigeons and doves, hornbills, and elsewhere birds of paradise, which disperse the seeds (Sinclair, 1958)

Wild nutmegs are an important food source for hornbills that select fruits with a single seed that are 10--25 mm diameter protected by a thick pericarp that dehisces when ripe to reveal the red or yellow-orange aril
Zoology 24 (2011) 137--147) found that in Peninsular Thailand Myristicaceae is the third most important family for hornbills, e.g. the Great and Wreathed Hornbills each fed on eight species

Among the nutmegs, fruits of Horsfieldia tomentosa and Myristica iners were consumed by five species of hornbill (Bushy-crested, Great, Helmeted, Wreathed and Wrinkled Hornbills) while Knema furfuracea, K. globularia and H. sucosa were visited by four, M. elliptica by three, Endocomia macrocoma by two, and Gymnacranthera farquhariana, H. irya, K. hookeriana and K. pseudolaurina each by one hornbill species
Eight nutmeg species have been reported to be consumed by primates (Norsham, Plants as Food for Animals in Peninsular Malaysia

Fruits and/or leaves of Horsfieldia irya were consumed by the Agile Gibbon, Banded Leaf Monkey and by Long-tailed and Pig-tailed Macaques, while Knema cinera was eaten by Siamang, Lar Gibbon and Pig-tailed Macaque
Fruits of four species, H. superba, K. furfuracea, K. glauca and K. intermedia are eaten by elephants (Norsham, 2005)
Squirrels have been observed eating seeds of at least nine nutmeg species, but while they may be an important food source for the squirrels, the seeds are likely to be destroyed

Dissemination by water may occur in Horsfieldia wallichii where the seed floats because of air trapped between aril and testa, and in H. irya, a widespread riverine species, that has cavities in the endosperm
The seed of the swamp nutmeg, Myristica elliptica, is reported to float (Sinclair (1958) p. 214), even without the aril
The recalcitrant seeds remain viable for a restricted period only, 30--75 (--315) days (Ng, Trop
Fruits, Seeds, Seedlings & Tr. (2014) 177--179), and germinate only in damp, shady environments
Therefore, the natural reestablishment of Myristicaceae in secondary forest is impossible.
In most myristicaceous species, the heartwood is poorly differentiated from the sapwood, and the wood is of minor commercial importance
The timber is suitable for temporary light constructions

The wood, mainly from the blackish-stemmed group (penarahan arang) in Myristica viz., M. cinnamomea, M. depressa, M. elliptica, M. gigantea, M. iners, M. lowiana, M. maingayi, M. maxima, and M. wyatt-smithii is mostly soft or moderately hard or heavy; perishable, but easily treated with preservatives; it is easy to work, but sometimes splits soon
The sapwood is pale, sometimes not well defined, but often the heartwood is dark reddish brown
The seed (with endosperm) of Myristica fragrans Houtt., is the nutmeg of commerce (buah pala), and the spicy aril around the seed is mace
The pericarp is candied and commonly for sale in Malaysia
The seeds of some species may be used for their fat content or their fragrance, or as medicine
A few species are ornamental, e.g. Horsfieldia iryaghedhi (Gaertner) Warb.
Myristicaceae is a homogeneous family and clearly belongs (also phyto-chemically) within the Magnoliales
It seems most related with Annonaceae, mainly through the ruminate endosperm, the foliage that is reminiscent of Annonaceae, and the 3-lobed perianth is remiscent of Lauraceae and Annonaceae
Myristicaceae are distinguished, however, by their unisexual flowers with a uniseriate perianth, and monocarpellate 1-ovuled female flowers
Phylogenetic analysis of the genera revealed that the family is monophyletic and of African origin (Sauquet, Phylogénie des Myristicaceae
Institut Agronomique (1998) Paris-Grignon), but according to recent cladistic analysis of all genera and related families by Sauquet et al. (Bot
Soc. 142 (2003) 125) and Stevens (Angiosperm Phylogeny Website, 2008), this family is as yet not properly placed as it falls beyond the recognised basal orders (APG crown-group of Magnoliales).

All members of Myristicaceae can be recognised in the field by their general habit, i.e. slender bole, with monopodial crown, the branches more-or-less verticillate and tiered, and the rather long exstipulate distichous leaves like those of Annonaceae
The latter family differs in its flower structure and fruit, and lacks the red exudate of the cut bark
Further differences are obvious in the transversely cut twig where the bark has radiating parenchyma in the Annonaceae, and also the pollen is different
The genera of Myristicaceae can be distinguished on vegetative characters only with experience; flower, inflorescence and fruit characters are necessary for a definite identification

Useful characters are the non-striate, usually finely lenticellate and granulate bark of the twigs in Gymnacranthera, or the dry leaves not readily breaking into pieces in most of Knema and Gymnacranthera
The male organ in unisexual flowers is formed by the fusion of a various number of stamens
Together they form the androecium, situated in the centre of the flowers
Each anther consists of a pair of lobes or locules (which are usually transversely septate when immature)
When fully fused, the number of anthers may be difficult to count, but it is half that of the often closely appressed locules
The Malesian genera all have (almost) completely fused stamens, forming an androecium whose shape is characteristic for the genus
For convenience sake, for each genus, schematic drawings with brief explanation of the construction of the androecium, and the terms used in the taxonomic text are given in Fig. 1 and below
The (partly) connate or free anthers are shown in solid black
In the case of connate anthers, these form the synandrium and the fused filaments below it form a stalk called the androphore
When the androphore is absent or inconspicuous, the synandrium coincides with the androecium
In Knema the anthers are mostly free, and the androecium is described in a different way
In the species descriptions the number of anthers is given in Endocomia, Gymnacranthera and Knema, but in Horsfieldia and Myristica only the number of anther locules.
